data.hypothesis: The measured two-target/128-thread candidate (0.002585 s) was faster than the four-target/128-thread selected parent (0.004165 s), while both were slower than baseline (0.001844 s); the two-target/256-thread trial was also slower (0.002745 s). Test an intermediate three-target mapping with 128 threads fixed, assigning 384 unique targets per block. Reusing each loaded source across three register-resident target accumulations may help relative to two targets, but added accumulators may raise register pressure and reduce occupancy. No speedup is assumed; the controller should assess correctness and all scored sizes.

memory_lessons.applicability: For this T2 campaign, compare coarsening factors and mappings with the official measurements; prior correctness does not establish a speedup.
memory_lessons.claim: The measured two-target/128-thread, four-target/128-thread, and two-target/256-thread candidates were all slower than baseline by recorded mean_seconds. The four-target candidate was slower than the two-target/128-thread candidate, but these measurements do not establish why.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure a three-target/128-thread mapping with items_per_block=384 after full correctness checks, and compare its scored-size results with baseline and prior coarsening candidates.

data.notes: This is a three-target-per-thread experiment with block=128 and items_per_block=384. The kernel independently guards targets in a partial final group, loads source position/mass values once per source iteration for reuse across target calculations, writes each valid target once, and uses no shared-memory source tiling. The supplied measurements cover prior candidates only; no new correctness or performance result is claimed.
transformations: Map each thread to up to three unique targets at offsets 0, blockDim.x, and 2*blockDim.x within its 384-target block group.
Load each source position and mass once per interaction-loop iteration and reuse those register values for the three valid target accumulations; keep each target's accumulators separate.
Guard targets independently in partial groups and write each valid output exactly once; use no shared-memory tiling or block-level multi-output assignment.
